answer_text:
Our honest answer has two parts, and they run in opposite directions.

First, what we can show you. Our record opens around the year 200 with a hard trace: a city chronicle drawn from real archives records that the great flood destroyed a church building in Edessa. That church building is our earliest dated trace, though we cannot be certain the line stood in the first record and was not added later. From that point forward the record is solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. When the sources begin, the practices are already there - assembly on the first day, fasting, the covenant already established enough to need correcting, the one Gospel already the standard. We lived our inheritance as apostolic, but our written record shows it only from the point where the sources begin.

Second, what we told ourselves. The beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus, and of Addai the apostle who came to heal him and set the church's life in order, is our cherished legend. It was written down generations later to give our church an apostolic beginning. We tell it as our legend, not as our history. It shows how we saw ourselves - a people whose faith went back to the apostles' own work. But it is not documentary evidence of how our practices began.

So the honest answer is this: what the record actually shows is practice older than proof. The practices were real when the sources begin. The chain connecting them backward to the apostles is what we believed and told, not what we can document for you. We would rather hand you that honest answer than claim a chain of evidence we do not have.

answer_text:
We held that judgment is real and is just, and that the Judge knows who comes gladly when the door is open. We said that Death has ruled everyone since Adam, without distinction, and that one Man broke into that kingdom and beat it. What waits beyond death is not a roster but the Judge, who repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction. Our teacher wrote that every man will receive his reward by his work. Those with a small fault the Judge will rebuke, and then he will give them the inheritance of life. He left the reckoning to the Judge himself.

What we did not do was draw the modern map of who exactly burns. Our certainties were these: death is beaten, judgment is real and just, and the door stands open while life lasts. We preached the warning as urgently as the hope. But our confidence lay in the Judge, not in a list of the excluded.

Now here is what honesty makes us say plainly. We drew real boundaries around ourselves. We answered Marcion, Bardaisan, and Mani by name, calling them deception. We would not share their communion. And our argument with the Jewish people among us was real, local, and bitter. Roughly four of our sage's letters carry that bitterness, and we saved only our own side. No answering voice was kept. We cannot promise you that our record was even-handed about difference. In that direction, plainly, it was not.

What we will not do is pretend we declared their eternal fate while we lived. That judgment we left where we said we left it: with the Judge.
